title: Identify and report common pests and diseases in plant propogation and landscapes

lessons.title: Common pests
lessons.html:
Common pests

A pest is an insect or animal that damages plants. If we find pests early, they are easy to control. If we leave them, they can kill many plants in the nursery or garden. Your job is to look, find and report.

Pests you will see

PestWhat it looks likeDamage
AphidsTiny green, black or grey insects in groups on new tipsCurled leaves, sticky leaves
MealybugsSmall white fluffy insectsWeak plants, sticky leaves
ScaleSmall brown or white bumps on stems and leavesYellow leaves, black sooty mould
WhiteflyTiny white flies that fly up when you shake the plantYellow leaves, sticky leaves
Red spider miteVery tiny; fine webs under leavesLeaves look dusty and speckled
CaterpillarsSoft worm-like larvae of moths and butterfliesHoles in leaves
Snails and slugsShiny trails on paths and leavesHoles in leaves, eaten seedlings
CutwormsGrey worms in the soilSeedlings cut off at the soil
Lily borerBlack and yellow caterpillars on clivias and amaryllisLeaves eaten, plants rot

Where to look

  • Under the leaves
  • On new soft tips and buds
  • On stems
  • In the soil at the base of plants

Sticky leaves and lots of ants often mean there are sucking insects like aphids, mealybugs or scale. Ants farm these insects for their sweet honeydew.

Check plants every day when you water. Walk slowly and turn over a few leaves on each bench or bed. Pests often start on a few plants in one corner and then spread. If you find them early, only a few plants need treatment.

lessons.title: Common diseases and how to report
lessons.html:
Common diseases and how to report

A plant disease is mostly caused by fungi, bacteria or viruses. Diseases spread fast when it is wet, warm and the plants are close together.

Diseases you will see

DiseaseSigns
Powdery mildewWhite powder on leaves, for example on roses
Black spotBlack spots on rose leaves, then yellow leaves fall
RustOrange or brown powdery spots under leaves
Damping offSeedlings fall over at the soil level
Root rotPlant wilts even when the soil is wet; brown soft roots
Grey mouldGrey fluffy mould on flowers and soft leaves

Not every problem is a pest or disease

Yellow leaves can also come from too much water, too little water, or hunger for fertiliser. Burnt leaf edges can come from wind, sun or too much fertiliser. Report what you see and let your team leader decide.

How to report

  1. Look closely. What do you see? Insects, spots, powder, holes, wilting?
  2. Note where: which plants, which block or bed, how many plants.
  3. If you can, take a photo with your phone, or bring a leaf in a closed bag.
  4. Tell your team leader the same day.
  5. Write it in the pest record book if there is one.

What you can do

  • Pick off snails and caterpillars by hand.
  • Remove and bag dead or very sick seedlings.
  • Keep sick plants apart from healthy plants.
  • Wash hands after touching sick plants, so you do not spread disease.

Never spray chemicals unless you are trained and your team leader allows it. Follow the label always.

Key points

  • Check plants every day, under leaves and on new tips.
  • Sticky leaves and ants often mean sucking insects.
  • Powder, spots and mould are signs of disease.
  • Report what, where and how many to your team leader the same day.
  • Do not spray unless you are trained and allowed.
